268 - Food & Philosophy - Eat, Think, an: This anthology takes eating seriously as a subject for philosophy, from Plato's account of why humans alone truly 'eat' rather than merely feed, through the learned banquets of ancient Greece and Rome, to the great cookbooks of Apicius and Artusi. Its essays ask what a proper meal owes to friendship, memory, and tradition, whether recipes are inventions or inherited wisdom, and how the pleasure of the table relates to the good life defended by Epicurus.
271 - Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyo: Fatherhood is an everyday role, but this collection shows how philosophically loaded it is: what makes a man a father, and what does being one ask of him? Philosophers and first-time dads bring Heidegger, Aristotle, Camus, and the ethics of care to bear on fatherhood's rituals, the identity of the 'man-child' of films like Knocked Up, tough-love figures from Darth Vader to Bambi's father, raising ethical children, and whether a life 'all about the kids' can still be the father's own meaningful life.
272 - Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyo: Motherhood is often treated as instinct or etiquette, but this anthology argues it is a site of real philosophical work. Its essays weigh whether lying to children can ever be justified (with help from Kant and Seinfeld's George Costanza), the ethics of breastfeeding and bodily autonomy, whether gender is hardwired or socially built, and what Simone de Beauvoir's idea of the 'ideal mother' as a social construction does to women who live under it.
273 - Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone: Sailing is slow, wet, uncomfortable, and occasionally lethal, which makes the devotion it inspires a genuine puzzle. This collection of essays by philosophers and lifelong sailors asks why people leave comfort behind to court the sea: what facing thirty-foot seas teaches about courage and self-worth, how tacking and capsizing train practical wisdom, and what solo ocean sailors like Bernard Moitessier found out alone on the water about presence, mastery, and meaning.
274 - Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone -: Coffee is a plant pesticide that billions of people drink on purpose, banned in Mecca in 1511 and celebrated in every city cafe since. This anthology follows the bean into philosophy: whether fair trade in coffee requires God to ground ethics, what a expert cupper's palate says about knowledge and taste, what the morning ritual reveals about Buddhist impermanence and craving, and how the coffeehouse became, from Socrates Cafes to neighborhood counters, a place where strangers learn to talk.
275 - Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone: Hunting forces the questions other pastimes can dodge: life, death, and what we owe animals. This anthology stages the debate on all sides, from David Petersen's defense of fair-chase restraint to the attack that the sportsman's own concern for a quick, clean kill, taken seriously, ends in not hunting at all. Along the way it weighs Peter Singer's case against sport hunting, the vegan-turned-deer-hunter who wanted to face killing directly, and what wolves and wilderness teach about belonging to a food chain.
277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - H: Pornography is watched by millions and condemned by nearly everyone else, and this anthology tries to think clearly about the whole business. Porn journalist Gram Ponante riffs on Plato's cave, a working performer asks whether porn damages her life, and other essays trace philosophy's old entanglement with erotic writing from the medieval 'Lay of Aristotle' to censorship arguments. The collection also looks hard at the cognitive science of watching, faked orgasms, and gay bareback porn read through AIDS and Freud.
278 - Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone: Fashion gets mocked as frivolous, but this collection argues it carries the zeitgeist, from Ugg boots to Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Olympic salute. Its essays ask what actually makes something fashionable, why 'cool' seems to collapse the moment its owner is caught trying (think James Dean versus the anxious tryhard), whether clothing can be autonomous art, and what Chanel perfume ads, Barbie play, and sweatshop labor reveal about desire, objectification, and the ethics of what we wear.
279 - Christmas – Philosophy for Everyon: Christmas began, its own historians argue, as a fourth-century compromise with the solstice, and the holiday has never fully resolved the tug-of-war between the manger and the sleigh. This anthology philosophizes the season: Hume's argument against miracles applied to the virgin birth and a theologian's reply, the pagan roots of the tree and of Santa, whether the Santa lie poisons parental honesty, the Foucauldian anxiety in a Santa who 'sees you when you're sleeping,' and whether the War on Christmas exists at all.
280 - Gardening – Philosophy for Everyon: Gardening looks like a hobby and this book treats it as a philosophy seminar in the soil. Its essays trace how Greeks and Romans made farming a school of virtue, how a seventeenth-century English estate balanced beauty with use, and whether plants themselves deserve moral consideration. Along the way it asks how patience, humility, and care for reality grow in the gardener alongside the vegetables, from Epicurus's tranquility to the modern 'grow your own' revival.
